The evaluation is broader than typical for this area, spanning medical, autonomous driving, and satellite imaging, with recent baselines, ablations, qualitative examples, confidence intervals for key metrics, and a computational cost comparison.

CARL-SSL is a meaningful extension of the model: the spectral JEPA-style objective is well matched to variable spectra, and the satellite experiment suggests useful transfer from hyperspectral pretraining to multispectral downstream data.
The manuscript is generally clear and includes helpful pseudocode and implementation details in the supplement.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate rather than transformative: many ingredients are adaptations of wavelength-aware embeddings, Perceiver/Q-Former-style learned queries, and JEPA/VICReg objectives. The repeated "first" and foundation-model framing is stronger than the evidence supports.

The strongest medical result relies on synthetic multispectral cameras generated from the same hyperspectral data, preserving spatial content and potentially overstating robustness to real cross-camera acquisition shifts.
Some real-world gains are modest. On HSICity, CARL/CARL-SSL improve over baselines, but confidence intervals overlap substantially with Hyve and the non-pretrained CARL gain is small.

Baseline fairness is not fully convincing across experiments: backbones and heads differ in places, private medical data limits reproducibility, and simple but strong alternatives such as wavelength interpolation/resampling, channel dropout, or set/Perceiver baselines are not thoroughly explored.

Ablations are useful but incomplete: the paper does not isolate spectral self-attention vs cross-attention, spectral vs spatial SSL losses, readout choices, initialization effects, channel subsampling effects, or robustness to inaccurate wavelength/bandpass metadata.

Reproducibility is only partial: code/release plans are not stated, training schedules and run counts are not fully specified, and the private medical dataset prevents independent verification of one major result.

strengths: The problem is well motivated: handling spectral cameras with different channel counts and wavelength responses is an important practical barrier for spectral image learning.

The paper evaluates across three application domains and includes comparisons to relevant recent methods such as HyperFree, Hyve, Spectral Adapter, and SpectralGPT+. The reported gains in the synthetic organ setting and the HSICity/Cityscapes transfer setting are promising.

weaknesses: The novelty is moderate rather than strong. The main ingredients, including Fourier features, latent query cross-attention, ViT-style spatial backbones, JEPA-style prediction, and VICReg losses, are largely established; the paper overstates several “first” claims relative to recent wavelength-aware and spectral foundation model work.

The evaluation does not fully substantiate the broad camera-agnostic/foundation-model claims. The strongest organ experiment relies on synthetic multispectral cameras derived from the same hyperspectral data, so it does not demonstrate real sensor transfer with independent acquisition artifacts, calibration differences, or illumination variation.

Baseline fairness is a major concern. Different methods are paired with different backbones and initializations in places, while CARL benefits from strong modern transformer backbones and pretrained weights. This makes it hard to isolate whether gains come from the proposed spectral encoder rather than architecture capacity or training setup.

The CARL-SSL contribution is under-evaluated. Gains are modest in the urban experiment, and the satellite experiment lacks key ablations such as CARL without SSL, spectral-only versus spatial-only SSL, matched pretraining data comparisons, and sensitivity to pretraining set size.

The real-world experiments are somewhat narrow: urban transfer is evaluated on a single HSI test dataset and satellite transfer on one downstream dataset. The paper does not test held-out real cameras across multiple sensors per domain, which is central to the claimed camera-agnostic robustness.

Reproducibility is limited by use of a private medical dataset, unclear code/data release plans, incomplete details on random seeds and confidence interval computation, and limited reporting of training cost/runtime. The method also has substantially higher FLOPs than several baselines, which weakens the scalability claim.
Overall, the paper is technically plausible and has useful empirical signals, but the evidence and positioning are not yet convincing enough for acceptance at a top-tier AI venue.
